subject: Computer Networking
title: IP Addresses Explained
description: Learn IP Addresses Explained in one minute.

hook.text: Every device on the internet needs a unique address. Without one, packets wouldn't know where to go.

buildup.text: An IP address is a number. IPv4 looks like 192.168.1.1 — four groups of digits separated by dots.

discovery.text: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses. That sounded like plenty in the 1980s. Now it's not enough.

twist.text: IPv6 uses 128 bits instead of 32, creating more addresses than there are atoms on Earth.

climax.text: Most devices today still use IPv4 with workarounds like NAT. Full IPv6 adoption is still in progress.

punchline.text: An IP address is just a mailing address for machines.

quiz.question: Why was IPv6 created?
options: IPv4 doesn't have enough addresses for all modern devices
IPv4 was too fast for old hardware

details.summary: IP addresses are numerical labels assigned to every device on a network. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses like 192.168.1.1, providing about 4.3 billion unique addresses. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses to provide a virtually unlimited supply.
details.whyItMatters: IP addresses are how devices find each other on the internet. IPv4 address exhaustion drove the adoption of IPv6 and technologies like NAT.
takeaways: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses with about 4.3 billion possible values
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses for virtually unlimited devices
IP addresses identify devices for routing and delivery

faq.question: Why are we running out of IPv4 addresses?
faq.answer: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, but the world has many more connected devices. Smartphones, IoT devices, and cloud servers all need addresses. Regional registries exhausted their pools years ago. NAT and IPv6 are the main solutions to this scarcity.

faq.question: Why hasn't everyone switched to IPv6 yet?
faq.answer: IPv6 is not backward compatible with IPv4. Both must run simultaneously during the transition. Many legacy systems only support IPv4. NAT solved the immediate address shortage, reducing urgency. The transition requires updating hardware, software, and operational practices everywhere.
